column1: How do you feel about reviving characters from the dead in books? Not in a zombie way. It’s a tricky topic, and my feelings are mixed. On one hand, reviving characters can feel like a cheap trick, especially if it’s done without consequence or proper setup. It can undermine the emotional weight of their death and make it seem like narrative stakes don’t really matter. I mean, if characters can just pop back to life whenever the plot needs them, what’s the point of investing in their journey? It’s like playing a game with cheat codes—it might be fun for a moment, but it robs the experience of its depth and authenticity.  On the other hand, if it’s done thoughtfully, reviving a character can open up fascinating possibilities. It can explore themes like second chances, the nature of life and death, or the consequences of tampering with the natural order. When it’s handled with care—say, through careful foreshadowing, established rules within the story’s universe, or a significant cost to the revival—it can add layers of complexity rather than detract from the narrative. I’m not opposed to the concept in principle, but it’s one of those things where execution is everything.  Take, for example, Gandalf’s return in *The Lord of the Rings*. It works because it’s not just a random resurrection—it’s tied to the lore of the world, his role as a Maia, and the greater stakes of the story. His return serves a purpose that goes beyond just keeping him around for convenience. But then you have instances in other stories where a character’s revival feels unearned, like the writers just wanted to retcon their death because fans were upset. That kind of approach usually leaves me rolling my eyes.  I think the key is to ask whether the revival serves the story or the audience. If it’s purely fan service or a way to avoid dealing with the fallout of a character’s death, it’s probably not worth it. But if it adds depth, complexity, or drives the narrative forward in a meaningful way, then it can be a powerful tool. Ultimately, like most things in storytelling, it all comes down to the *why* and the *how*. Done right, it can be brilliant. Done poorly, it can ruin an otherwise solid story.

What do atheists think the evolution of atheism will be like in the year 2050? Predicting the evolution of atheism by 2050 is tricky, not because of atheism itself, but because societal, cultural, and technological changes are so unpredictable. That said, I’d expect atheism to continue growing, especially in regions where access to education and information is increasing. As people become more scientifically literate and less tethered to traditional religious structures, the trend toward secularism will likely persist. But it’s not just about rejecting religion—it’s also about the rise of alternative worldviews. Atheism might evolve to coexist with or even morph into broader philosophical systems like humanism, skepticism, or even forms of spirituality that don’t involve a deity.   One key factor will be the role of technology. The internet has already democratized access to information, making it easier for people to question religious dogma and connect with like-minded thinkers. By 2050, advancements in AI, virtual reality, and space exploration could further challenge traditional religious narratives. Imagine a world where virtual reality allows people to experience a fully immersive simulation of the universe’s origins, complete with scientific explanations. Or consider how the discovery of extraterrestrial life might reshape humanity’s place in the cosmos and, by extension, its relationship with religion. These developments could accelerate the shift toward atheism or secularism.  However, it’s not all smooth sailing. Religion has proven incredibly resilient, often adapting to cultural changes rather than disappearing outright. In some parts of the world, particularly where religion is deeply intertwined with identity or politics, atheism might face resistance or even hostility. And while atheism is growing in the West, it’s important to recognize that global trends aren’t uniform. In some regions, religious revivalism or fundamentalism could counteract secular progress.  Another wildcard is the role of younger generations. Gen Z and Gen Alpha are growing up in a world where atheism is more normalized, but they’re also navigating unprecedented challenges—climate change, political instability, and economic uncertainty. These pressures could drive some toward religion as a source of comfort or community, while others might find solace in secular philosophies that emphasize reason and human agency.   Ultimately, atheism in 2050 will likely be more diverse and nuanced than it is today. It might not even be called “atheism” anymore, as the term itself is defined in opposition to theism. Instead, we might see a broader spectrum of non-religious beliefs, from hardline scientific materialism to more eclectic, individualized worldviews. What’s certain is that the conversation will continue, shaped by the same forces that have always driven human thought—curiosity, skepticism, and the search for meaning in a complex universe.

Why are some women so worried about not being able to access abortion in America when all they need to do if they don’t want kids at the moment is to keep their legs closed or be careful with birth control? It’s not as simple as “keeping their legs closed” or relying solely on birth control. Life is messy, unpredictable, and full of circumstances that don’t fit neatly into a one-size-fits-all solution. Birth control isn’t foolproof—it can fail, even when used correctly. Condoms break, pills can be missed, and IUDs can shift. And let’s not forget that not everyone has equal access to contraception in the first place. For some women, especially those in low-income or rural areas, getting reliable birth control can be a logistical and financial nightmare.    Then there’s the issue of sexual assault. No one chooses to be raped, yet it happens far too often. Should a survivor be forced to carry a pregnancy to term because someone else decided to violate her body? That’s not just unfair—it’s cruel.    Even in consensual relationships, things can go wrong. A partner might lie about using protection or pressure someone into sex without it. Relationships can be complicated, and not every woman has the power or agency to enforce her boundaries perfectly every single time.    And what about women who *do* want kids someday, just not right now? Life doesn’t always go according to plan. A woman might be in school, starting a career, or dealing with financial instability. She might already have children and know she can’t afford another. Or she might be in an abusive relationship and realize bringing a child into that environment would be disastrous.    Abortion isn’t something anyone takes lightly. It’s a deeply personal decision, often made under immense stress and with careful consideration. The idea that women are just being careless or irresponsible is a gross oversimplification. It ignores the complexities of human life and the very real challenges women face.    At the end of the day, it’s about autonomy—the right to make decisions about your own body. No one should be forced to carry a pregnancy against their will, regardless of the circumstances. It’s not about encouraging abortion; it’s about ensuring that women have the freedom to make the best choice for themselves and their futures. And that’s something worth fighting for.

Maybe a biology teach in a public school can’t teach the truth about the existence of life. But can she point out the fallacies of evolution without speaking about creationism? Is that unconstitutional? It’s a nuanced issue, but yes, a biology teacher can address misconceptions or fallacies in evolutionary theory without diving into creationism. The key is to stick to the science. Evolution, as a scientific theory, is open to scrutiny and refinement—that’s how science progresses. For example, a teacher could discuss transitional fossils, genetic mutations, or the mechanisms of natural selection, pointing out common misunderstandings or oversimplifications. What they can’t do is promote religious ideologies under the guise of science, as that would violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment. Public schools are secular institutions, and while they can’t endorse religion, they also can’t actively discredit it. The line is drawn when the discussion moves from scientific critique to doctrinal debate. For instance, a teacher might explain why certain “gaps” in the fossil record don’t disprove evolution but instead reflect incomplete data or the rarity of fossilization. They could also explore examples of convergent evolution or vestigial structures to illustrate how complex traits can arise gradually. However, if the critique shifts to implying that evolution is inherently flawed because it contradicts a religious text, that’s crossing the line. The Constitution ensures that public education remains neutral on matters of faith, allowing students to form their own beliefs without coercion. So, while it’s entirely appropriate to teach the scientific process, including questioning and refining theories, it’s unconstitutional to use that as a platform to promote or undermine religious views. It’s a delicate balance, but one that’s essential for maintaining both academic integrity and religious freedom.

What grade did you learn Darwin’s theory of evolution? I first encountered Darwin’s theory of evolution in middle school, around 7th grade, though it was presented in a very simplified form. We learned the basics—natural selection, survival of the fittest, and how species change over time. It was fascinating, but it wasn’t until high school biology that the concept really clicked for me. That’s when we dove into the mechanisms of evolution, like genetic mutations, gene flow, and genetic drift. I remember being particularly struck by the idea that small, incremental changes over millions of years could lead to the incredible diversity of life we see today. It was one of those moments where the world suddenly made a lot more sense.    In college, as an engineering student, I didn’t study evolution directly, but the principles of adaptation and optimization resonated with me. Engineering, after all, is about solving problems through iterative design and improvement, which isn’t all that different from how evolution works. I’ve always appreciated how Darwin’s theory ties together so many fields—biology, genetics, geology, even philosophy. It’s a framework that explains not just how life changes, but why it’s so resilient and adaptable.    Even now, as an adult, I find myself revisiting the topic, whether it’s through books, documentaries, or discussions with friends. It’s one of those ideas that keeps giving the more you think about it. And while I’m not a biologist, I’ve come to see evolution as one of the most elegant and powerful explanations for the natural world. It’s a reminder that even the most complex systems can arise from simple, gradual processes—a lesson that’s as relevant in engineering as it is in biology.
